questions.q: 1 a) Define software project management?
questions.a: Software project management is the application of knowledge, skills, tools and methods to plan, organise, estimate, schedule and control software development activities so that the project is completed on time, within budget and at the required quality. Its main activities are project planning, size and effort estimation, risk management, scheduling, resource allocation, progress monitoring and quality assurance. Because software is intangible and changes easily, the manager must rely on estimates and visibility tools rather than on physical inspection. The overall goal is to deliver a product that satisfies customer needs while keeping cost, schedule and quality under control.
questions.explanation: This is the standard definition of software project management and names its core activities and goal, which is what a two-mark definition question expects.
questions.oneShotPreview: Planning, estimating, scheduling and controlling software work to deliver on time, on budget and to quality.

questions.q: 1 b) Identify skills necessary for Managing Software Projects.
questions.a: A software project manager needs both technical and managerial skills. Technical skills include knowledge of software life cycle models, estimation methods (LOC, Function Points, COCOMO), risk analysis, testing and software quality practices. Managerial skills include leadership, team building, communication, negotiation, decision-making, planning, scheduling and budgeting. The manager should also understand the customer's application domain and be able to use project-tracking tools. Above all, the manager must balance people, process and product concerns and resolve conflicts within the team.
questions.explanation: The answer lists the technical, managerial and domain skill groups that standard texts associate with an effective software project manager.
questions.oneShotPreview: Technical (lifecycle, estimation, risk, quality) + managerial (leadership, communication, planning) + domain knowledge.

questions.q: 1 c) What are the three stages of COCOMO estimation technique and express general form of the COCOMO.
questions.a: COCOMO (Constructive Cost Model) has three stages. (1) Basic COCOMO: a static model that estimates effort and schedule from program size in KLOC using only a set of constants. (2) Intermediate COCOMO: adds an effort adjustment factor built from 15 cost drivers covering product, hardware, personnel and project attributes. (3) Detailed COCOMO: applies those cost drivers separately at each phase of the life cycle using a hierarchical, three-level model. The general form is Effort = a x (KLOC)^b person-months, where a and b depend on the project class: organic (2.4, 1.05), semi-detached (3.0, 1.12) and embedded (3.6, 1.20). Development time and average staffing are then derived from the effort estimate.
questions.explanation: It names all three COCOMO stages and gives the standard effort formula with the usual constants, matching the question's two requirements.
questions.oneShotPreview: Basic, Intermediate, Detailed; Effort = a x (KLOC)^b person-months.

questions.q: 1 d) Name the characteristics of a Good SRS Document.
questions.a: A good Software Requirements Specification (SRS) should be correct, complete, consistent, unambiguous, verifiable, modifiable, traceable and testable. It must be precise and easy to read, have a clear structure and state the scope explicitly. It should avoid over-specification (design details) and incompleteness (unresolved TBDs), and should distinguish functional from non-functional requirements. It should also be stable enough to serve as a baseline, prioritised, and allow each requirement to be traced to its source and later to design, code and test cases.
questions.explanation: These are the classic qualities of a good SRS listed in software engineering texts, with a short clarification of the key ones.
questions.oneShotPreview: Correct, complete, consistent, unambiguous, verifiable, modifiable, traceable and testable.

questions.q: 1 e) What is a Formal Technique?
questions.a: A formal technique is a mathematically rigorous method for specifying, developing and verifying software, based on a notation with precisely defined syntax and semantics. It uses formal specification languages such as Z, VDM, B, algebraic or axiomatic specifications, and temporal logic to describe a system without ambiguity. Because the specification is mathematical, one can reason about it and even prove that an implementation satisfies it. Formal techniques are used mainly for safety-critical and high-reliability systems; their benefits are precision and provable correctness, while their drawbacks are high cost, extra effort and a steep learning curve.
questions.explanation: The answer defines formal methods by their mathematical basis and notation, and notes where they are used and their trade-offs.
questions.oneShotPreview: Math-based rigorous specification and verification; precise and provable but costly and hard to learn.

questions.q: 2 a) Discuss Few points about project size? What are the popular metrics to measure project size? How can the size of a project be estimated during the project planning stage?
questions.a: Project size is a primary input to effort, cost and schedule estimation: larger projects require more effort and time, and the relationship is nonlinear because large projects add communication and integration overhead. The popular size metrics are Lines of Code (LOC, usually expressed in KLOC), which counts delivered source lines, and Function Points (FP), which measure functionality from counts of inputs, outputs, inquiries, files and interfaces. Other measures include use-case points, story points and number of functions or transactions. During planning, size is estimated from the requirements or SRS by analogy with similar completed projects, by expert judgement or Delphi, by counting functions/use cases and converting them using a productivity ratio, or by building a prototype to reduce uncertainty. The estimate is refined as design details become available.
questions.explanation: It explains why size matters, names the two main metrics and gives the practical early-estimation methods used during planning.
questions.oneShotPreview: Size drives effort/cost; metrics LOC and FP; estimate from the SRS by analogy, experts or function/use-case counts.

questions.q: 2 b) Identify and explain factors contributing to the complexity of managing a software project.
questions.a: Software projects are complex because the product is intangible and its progress is visible only through documents and code. Major contributing factors are large project size, unclear or frequently changing requirements, use of new or unfamiliar technology, a new application domain, distributed or heterogeneous teams, tight schedules and budgets, high reliability and quality demands, and many stakeholders with conflicting interests. Estimation uncertainty and the difficulty of measuring real progress add further problems, as does the need to coordinate many interdependent tasks. If these factors are not controlled, they lead to cost and schedule overruns and poor quality, which is why risk and change management are essential.
questions.explanation: The answer identifies the standard complexity factors and explains why each makes management harder.
questions.oneShotPreview: Intangibility, changing requirements, size, new technology, distributed teams, tight deadlines and many stakeholders.

questions.q: 3 a) List the important shortcomings of LOC metric when used as a software size metric for carrying out project estimations.
questions.a: LOC is simple to count but has several serious drawbacks as an estimation metric. It is language-dependent: a line of code in a high-level language does not represent the same work as a line in assembly, so it unfairly penalises high-level languages and concise design. It measures implementation rather than functionality, so it rewards code bloat and discourages reuse, refactoring and short solutions. It is hard to estimate early because coding details are unknown during planning. It is sensitive to comments, blank lines and individual coding style, and different counting conventions give different numbers. It also ignores complexity, data and interfaces, and works poorly for object-oriented, generated or non-procedural software.
questions.explanation: This is the standard critique of LOC as a size metric: language bias, late availability, style dependence and poor link to functionality.
questions.oneShotPreview: Language-dependent, rewards bloat, measures code not function, hard to estimate early, style-sensitive, ignores complexity.

questions.q: 3 b) Demonstrate the Responsibilities of a software project manager? Explain it.
questions.a: A software project manager plans the project and estimates its size, effort, cost and schedule, then allocates resources and forms the team. They assign tasks, set milestones and monitor actual progress against the plan, taking corrective action when there is a deviation. They identify and mitigate risks, control quality and manage changes to requirements. They act as the interface with the customer and other stakeholders, reporting status, negotiating scope and handling expectations. They also provide the team with the required environment, tools and support, and ensure that deliverables meet the agreed standards. In short, the manager is accountable for delivering the product on time, within budget and at the required quality.
questions.explanation: It covers the planning, organising, leading and controlling responsibilities of a project manager as described in standard texts.
questions.oneShotPreview: Plans, estimates, staffs, schedules, monitors, manages risk/quality/change and reports to stakeholders.

questions.q: 4 a) Compare the following project size estimation techniques. i) Expert judgement ii) Delphi technique.
questions.a: Expert judgement asks one or a few experienced people to estimate project size from their memory of similar completed projects. It is quick and cheap but can be biased, subjective and dominated by one person's opinion. The Delphi technique is a structured, group form of expert judgement: several experts estimate independently and anonymously, a moderator circulates the estimates and reasons, and further rounds are held until a consensus is reached. Delphi reduces the influence of dominant personalities and groupthink and is generally more accurate, but it takes more time. Both techniques rely on human experience rather than a formula and work best when comparable historical project data exists; Delphi is essentially a more disciplined, iterative version of expert judgement.
questions.explanation: The comparison covers method, number of participants, bias, time and accuracy, and correctly identifies Delphi as structured expert judgement.
questions.oneShotPreview: Expert judgement = one/few experts, fast but biased; Delphi = anonymous multi-round consensus, slower and more reliable.

questions.q: 4 b) Interpret an overview of the different categories of estimation techniques.
questions.a: Software estimation techniques can be grouped into several categories. Analogous or top-down estimation compares the new project with similar past projects and scales by size or complexity. Expert judgement and Delphi rely on the experience of one or more experts. Bottom-up estimation decomposes the work into small tasks, estimates each one and sums them. Parametric or algorithmic models use a formula, such as COCOMO or Function Points, to derive effort from size and cost drivers. Model-based or machine-learning approaches use historical project data to build a predictive model. Each category involves a trade-off: top-down is fast but coarse, bottom-up is detailed but time-consuming, and algorithmic models are repeatable but need calibration. In practice several techniques are used together and the results cross-checked.
questions.explanation: It lists the standard categories of estimation techniques and states their relative strengths and weaknesses.
questions.oneShotPreview: Analogous, expert/Delphi, bottom-up, parametric (COCOMO/FP) and model-based — fast vs detailed, coarse vs calibrated.

questions.q: 5 Explain in detail the following project size estimation techniques. i) Lines of Code (LOC) ii) Function Point (FP) Metric
questions.a:
i) Lines of Code (LOC): LOC counts the number of source code lines delivered in a program, normally expressed in KLOC (thousands of lines), usually excluding comments and blank lines. Because effort and schedule grow with the amount of code to be written, LOC is a simple, automatable size measure and is the size input to basic COCOMO. It can be estimated early by analogy, by counting functions or use cases and applying a lines-per-function ratio, or through expert judgement. Its weaknesses are that it is language-dependent, penalises high-level languages, reuse and concise design, measures implementation rather than user functionality, is difficult to estimate before design, is sensitive to coding style and counting conventions, and ignores complexity, data and interfaces. It also encourages bloated code. 

ii) Function Point (FP) Metric: Function Point analysis measures the functional size of a system from the user's viewpoint, independent of programming language. It counts five component types: External Inputs (EI), External Outputs (EO), External Inquiries (EQ), Internal Logical Files (ILF) and External Interface Files (EIF). Each item is rated simple, average or complex and given a weight; the total is the Unadjusted Function Point (UFP) count. A Value Adjustment Factor based on 14 general system characteristics (data communications, performance, transaction rate, etc.) gives FP = UFP x (0.65 + 0.01 x sum of the 14 ratings). FP can be estimated from the requirements early, is language-independent and reflects user value, but the counting is somewhat subjective and requires trained people. FP values can be converted to equivalent LOC for use in effort models.
questions.explanation: This gives a detailed treatment of both techniques: counting rules, formulas, estimation use and advantages/limitations of each, as required by a ten-mark question.
questions.oneShotPreview: LOC = source lines (KLOC), simple but language-dependent; FP = weighted EI/EO/EQ/ILF/EIF x VAF, language-independent functional size.

questions.q: 6 Define Risk Management and Explain types of risk management?
questions.a: Risk management is the systematic process of identifying, analysing, prioritising and mitigating risks that could prevent a software project from achieving its goals. It is proactive: it tries to reduce the probability and impact of adverse events before they happen rather than reacting to crises. Its activities are risk identification, risk analysis (estimating probability and impact), risk prioritisation, mitigation planning, risk resolution and continuous risk monitoring. Risks are commonly classified as project risks (budget, schedule, staffing, resources, scope), technical risks (design, implementation, technology, complexity, changing requirements), business risks (market, legal, contractual, third parties) and product risks (defects, performance, usability). They are also described as known risks, predictable risks and unpredictable risks, the last needing contingency plans. Mitigation strategies are to avoid the risk, transfer it, reduce it or accept it; a risk management plan records the likely risks, their indicators, owners and responses.
questions.explanation: It defines risk management, lists its activities, the main risk categories and the standard mitigation strategies, which is what the question asks for.
questions.oneShotPreview: Identify, analyse, prioritise, mitigate and monitor risks; types: project, technical, business and known/predictable/unpredictable.

questions.q: 7 a) Analyze the concept of COCOMO model and its extension.
questions.a: COCOMO (Constructive Cost Model), proposed by Boehm, is an empirical algorithmic model that estimates effort and schedule from program size. Basic COCOMO uses Effort = a x (KLOC)^b person-months, with a and b set by project class: organic (2.4, 1.05), semi-detached (3.0, 1.12) and embedded (3.6, 1.20); development time is TDEV = c x (Effort)^d and average staffing = Effort / TDEV. Intermediate COCOMO multiplies the estimate by an effort adjustment factor derived from 15 cost drivers (product, hardware, personnel and project attributes), and Detailed COCOMO applies them phase by phase. Its main extension is COCOMO II, designed for modern iterative, object-oriented and reuse-oriented development. COCOMO II has three models: Application Composition (point-based for prototypes), Early Design (use-case points with 7 scale factors and 17 effort multipliers) and Post-Architecture (full model with 22 effort multipliers and 5 scale factors). Its general form is PM = A x Size^E x product(EM), where E represents the diseconomy of scale, and it supports incremental development and reused code.
questions.explanation: It explains the original model's formula and classes and then describes COCOMO II and its three sub-models, covering both parts of the question.
questions.oneShotPreview: COCOMO effort = a(KLOC)^b; COCOMO II = A x Size^E x product(EM) for iterative, reuse-based projects.

questions.q: 7 b) Evaluate the analytical technique 'Halstead's Software Science' with example
questions.a: Halstead's software science is an analytical, white-box metric that treats a program as a set of operators and operands and derives its size, complexity and effort from the source code. Its basic counts are n1 (distinct operators), n2 (distinct operands), N1 (total operator occurrences) and N2 (total operand occurrences). From these it computes vocabulary n = n1 + n2, length N = N1 + N2, estimated length = n1 log2(n1) + n2 log2(n2), volume V = N log2(n) bits, difficulty D = (n1/2) x (N2/n2), effort E = D x V, and estimated delivered bugs B = V / 3000. For example, for a tiny routine with operators main, int, =, + and ; (n1 = 5, N1 = 7) and operands a, b, c (n2 = 3, N2 = 5), we get n = 8, N = 12, V = 12 log2(8) = 36 bits and D = (5/2) x (5/3) about 4.17, giving E about 150. Evaluation: the metrics are objective, language-independent and automatically computable, and useful for comparing programs and studying productivity. However, they can only be applied after coding, ignore control flow, algorithm quality and user functionality, and their empirically derived formulas correlate weakly with real effort, so they are mostly a research and quality-analysis tool.
questions.explanation: It defines the Halstead measures and formulas, works through a small counted example and then evaluates strengths and limitations, satisfying an evaluate-with-example question.
questions.oneShotPreview: Counts operators/operands to get volume V = N log2(n) and effort E = D x V; objective but code-only and late.

questions.q: 8 a) Illustrate basic classes of software development projects with examples.
questions.a: Software development projects fall into several basic classes. (1) Generic software products built for a mass market by a vendor, such as a word processor or a mobile app, where customers are unknown at development time. (2) Custom or contracted systems built for a specific client, such as a bank's online banking system or a hospital information system, where the customer defines the requirements. (3) Embedded and real-time systems, such as aircraft flight control, automotive engine control or medical devices, where software is part of a larger hardware system with safety and timing constraints. (4) System software such as operating systems, compilers, database systems and device drivers. (5) Web and distributed applications such as e-commerce sites and cloud services. (6) Research or prototype projects and maintenance/re-engineering projects. Projects are also classed as organic, semi-detached or embedded in COCOMO. The classes differ in requirements stability, quality demands, risk and the development process used.
questions.explanation: It lists the main classes with concrete examples and notes how they differ, matching the two-mark-per-class marking scheme.
questions.oneShotPreview: Generic products, custom/contract, embedded/real-time, system software, web/distributed and prototypes — differing risks and processes.

questions.q: 8 b) Describe the main activities carried out during requirements analysis and specification phase? Explain it.
questions.a: The requirements analysis and specification phase converts a vague user need into a precise, documented specification. Its main activities are: (1) Requirements elicitation, gathering needs from customers, users and other stakeholders by interviews, questionnaires, observation, workshops and prototyping. (2) Analysis and negotiation, classifying requirements as functional or non-functional, checking feasibility, consistency and completeness, resolving conflicts and setting priorities. (3) Specification, documenting the agreed requirements in an SRS using natural language, structured notation, use cases or a formal specification. (4) Requirements validation, reviewing the SRS with the customer to confirm it is correct, complete, unambiguous, verifiable and traceable. (5) Requirements management, controlling changes and maintaining traceability throughout the project. A prototype is often built to clarify uncertain requirements. The outcome is an approved SRS that forms the basis for design and a contract between customer and developer.
questions.explanation: The answer names and explains the standard five activities of requirements engineering and states the phase's outcome.
questions.oneShotPreview: Elicit, analyse and negotiate, specify in an SRS, validate with the customer, then manage changes.

questions.q: 9 a) Identify and illustrate the important uses of a well-formulated SRS document.
questions.a: A well-formulated SRS has many important uses. It acts as a contract between customer and developer by stating what the system will do. It is the basis for design, coding and testing: test cases are derived directly from the requirements. It supports effort, cost and schedule estimation and project planning. It enables verification and validation because every requirement can be checked and tested. It improves communication among stakeholders, serves as a training document for new team members, and supports maintenance, enhancement and porting. It also provides a baseline for change control through requirements traceability. For example, when a customer requests a change, the SRS is consulted to see which functions and tests are affected.
questions.explanation: It enumerates the standard uses of an SRS and illustrates them with concrete examples such as test derivation and change control.
questions.oneShotPreview: Contract, basis for design/test, estimation, validation, communication, training, maintenance and change control.

questions.q: 9 b) Contrast the following categories of requirements. i) Functional requirements ii) Non-functional requirements
questions.a: Functional requirements state what the system must do: the functions, inputs, processing and outputs, for example 'the system shall allow a user to log in' or 'the system shall generate a monthly report'. They describe observable behaviour, can be mapped to use cases and are tested for correctness. Non-functional requirements state how the system behaves, that is, its quality attributes and constraints, such as response time under two seconds, security, reliability, availability, usability, maintainability, portability and standards compliance. They apply to the system as a whole rather than to one function and are often called quality-of-service requirements. Functional requirements are comparatively easy to specify and verify, while non-functional ones need measurable targets and are harder to test. Both belong in the SRS, and non-functional requirements strongly influence architectural decisions, for example adding a cache to meet a performance target.
questions.explanation: It contrasts the two categories by what they describe, scope, verifiability and design impact, which is what a contrast question requires.
questions.oneShotPreview: Functional = what the system does; non-functional = how well (performance, security, reliability, usability).

questions.q: 10 a) What is a Formal Technique? Identify important concepts in formal methods, and examine the merits and demerits of using formal techniques
questions.a: A formal technique is a rigorously mathematical approach to specifying, developing and verifying software using a language with precisely defined syntax and semantics. Important concepts in formal methods are: formal specification languages such as Z, VDM, B, algebraic and axiomatic specifications and temporal logic; a specification as a mathematical model of the system; refinement, the stepwise transformation of a specification into code with correctness preserved at each step; and verification or proof that the implementation satisfies the specification. Approaches are either model-oriented (describing state and operations, e.g. Z) or property-oriented (describing behaviour by axioms and equations). Merits are precision, absence of ambiguity, early detection of inconsistencies, the ability to prove correctness, higher reliability and a solid basis for testing. Demerits are a steep learning curve, high cost and time, need for specialist skills, difficulty with large or rapidly changing systems, limited tool support and weak direct connection to user needs, so formal methods are used mainly in safety-critical domains.
questions.explanation: The answer defines formal techniques, names the key concepts and then explicitly examines both merits and demerits.
questions.oneShotPreview: Math-based specification with refinement and proof; precise and provable but expensive, slow and specialist.

questions.q: 10 b) What is Axiomatic Specification? How to develop an axiomatic specification with an example
questions.a: Axiomatic specification is a property-oriented formal method that defines a system or abstract data type by a set of axioms: logical statements describing the properties its operations must satisfy, rather than by an algorithm or a state model. To develop one: (1) identify the abstract type and its operations; (2) define the signature, that is the sorts and operation names with their argument and result types; (3) write axioms giving the meaning of each operation, including base cases and general rules; (4) check the axioms for consistency and completeness; and (5) use them for reasoning about or verifying an implementation. For example, a stack with operations empty, push, pop, top and isempty can be specified by the axioms: isempty(empty) = true, isempty(push(s,x)) = false, top(push(s,x)) = x, and pop(push(s,x)) = s. These axioms completely characterise stack behaviour without saying how the stack is implemented.
questions.explanation: It defines axiomatic specification, gives the development steps and illustrates them with the classic stack axioms, covering both parts of the question.
questions.oneShotPreview: Define type, operations and logical axioms; e.g. top(push(s,x)) = x and pop(push(s,x)) = s for a stack.

questions.q: 11 Explain in details Algebraic Specification. Identify Pros and Cons of algebraic specifications with an example.
questions.a: Algebraic specification is a property-oriented formal method that specifies an abstract data type (ADT) or component by giving its syntax (sorts and operations) and its semantics as a set of equations or axioms over terms. It describes what the operations do rather than how they are implemented. A specification has a signature listing the sorts and operation symbols with their arities, and equational axioms defining their behaviour; specifications can be built incrementally by enrichment and instantiation, and properties are proved by equational reasoning or term rewriting. Example - a Stack ADT: sorts Stack, Integer, Boolean; operations empty -> Stack, push(Stack, Integer) -> Stack, pop(Stack) -> Stack, top(Stack) -> Integer, isempty(Stack) -> Boolean; axioms: isempty(empty) = true, isempty(push(s,x)) = false, top(push(s,x)) = x, pop(push(s,x)) = s, and top(empty) = error. Any correct implementation must satisfy these equations. Pros: precise and unambiguous, implementation-independent, supports verification, theorem proving and test generation, encourages clean abstract design, suits reusable ADTs, and can be executed as a term-rewriting prototype. Cons: hard and time-consuming to write, requires mathematical skill, large specifications become complex, poorly captures non-functional aspects such as performance and concurrency, limited industrial tool support, and can be overkill for ordinary projects.
questions.explanation: This is a detailed answer: it defines algebraic specification, explains its structure, gives a complete worked stack example and lists both pros and cons as a ten-mark question requires.
questions.oneShotPreview: ADT spec = signature + equational axioms (e.g. pop(push(s,x)) = s); precise and verifiable but hard, slow and weak on non-functional aspects.
